question: If 14 of 20 deaths fall in the week after a holiday, were the dying holding on for it?
answer: Not that the big records show. Small studies found deaths dipping before Passover or a birthday, but a few hundred deaths can draw a dip by chance alone. Ohio's 309,221 cancer deaths from 1989 to 2000 showed no drop before Christmas, Thanksgiving or the patient's birthday.
move: Before believing a pattern, ask how many cases drew it.
ask: Which story do I believe that rests on a handful of cases?

scene.hit: In the week after the date
notes: 14 of 20 died after the date: 70%. Pure chance; no effect is built in.
Ten times the deaths, still 57% after. A dip you could publish.
At 2,000 it is 52%. The pattern is melting into the truth, 50%.
Twenty thousand deaths. Before and after are level.
As many as Ohio's real study. Its records found no dip either.

reference: Young & Hade, Holidays, birthdays, and postponement of cancer death, JAMA 292(24):3012-3016, 2004

question: Red came up 8 times in 10 spins. Is the wheel favouring red?
answer: Almost surely not. On a European wheel 18 of 37 pockets are red: 48.6%. Ten spins swing wildly; 8 or more reds turn up in about one run of 10 in 22. Only thousands of spins pin the rate down, so a casino trusts its edge and a player should not trust a streak.
move: Judge a rate by thousands of tries, not by the last ten.
ask: What am I calling a trend that is ten tries long?

notes: Eight reds in ten: 80%. The wheel is fair; this is a simulation of chance.
A hundred spins and still 60% red. Enough to start a system.
A thousand spins: 51.2%. The streak is fading.
Ten thousand: 49.2%, a hair above the truth.
A hundred thousand: 48.7%, next to 18 in 37. Every fair wheel ends here.

reference: Epstein, The Theory of Gambling and Statistical Logic, 2nd edition, Academic Press, 2009

question: Aspirin saved lives after heart attacks, except, it seemed, for Geminis and Libras. Why?
answer: Chance, sliced thin. The ISIS-2 trial gave 17,187 heart-attack patients aspirin or a dummy pill; vascular deaths in five weeks fell from 11.8% to 9.4%. Split by star sign, on purpose, Geminis and Libras showed no benefit. Any small slice of a trial can swing that far. The authors' point was about subgroups, not stars.
move: Distrust an effect found in one slice of a study.
ask: Which result am I trusting that came from a small slice of the data?

notes: 200 patients, and aspirin looks deadly: 17% against 11%. Simulated chance.
1,000 patients. Aspirin still looks worse: 12.6% against 9.2%.
2,864, a sixth of the trial, about two star signs' worth. No benefit yet.
All 17,187: 9.4% against 11.8%, as in the real trial. Aspirin saves lives.

reference: ISIS-2 Collaborative Group, Randomised trial of intravenous streptokinase, oral aspirin, both, or neither among 17,187 cases of suspected acute myocardial infarction, The Lancet 2(8607):349-360, 1988
